reason: The borrowing is real and it is adjudicated at Mosiah 4:2, where the phrase first enters this assembly. 'With one voice' occurs in two KJV verses and only Exodus 24:3 is a covenant ratification, which is what makes it worth having; but Mosiah 5:2's use is the same narrator using his own formula eight verses later, not a fresh contact with Exodus. Registered here so that a reader who meets the phrase at 5:2 — where it is followed by 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us', the answering half of Exodus 24:3's 'All the words which the LORD hath said will we do' — is sent to the link at 4:2 rather than shown nothing.

A five-word run and an exact opposition. Jeremiah 44:16 is the people of Judah in Egypt refusing the prophet: 'As for the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the LORD, we will not hearken unto thee.' Mosiah 5:2 is a people accepting one: 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us.' The shared clause is the formula for reporting a prophet's speech back to him, and the KJV supplies it to a refusal and the Book of Mormon to an assent. Filed at length because the run is long enough to tempt and because the register's best entries are the ones where a real string match points the wrong way.

sharedText: make a covenant with our God
reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate, at 3.00, and a fair one: Ezra 10:3 is a covenant made with God by an assembled people, which is exactly the scene. It is declined because 'a covenant with our God' is the KJV's ordinary phrase for the transaction and because Ezra's covenant is to put away foreign wives, a subject with no counterpart anywhere in Benjamin's sermon. Where the wording is the standard idiom for the act being performed, the parallel is a description of the act and not evidence of a source. The verse's real borrowing is in its second half, at Revelation 14:10-11.

sharedText: take heed that ye do not
reason: 'Take heed that ye do not' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 6:1, which makes this the kind of candidate that ought to be argued rather than dropped — and the context is more tempting still, since Matthew 6:1 governs the almsgiving instruction that Mosiah 4:16-26 has just been rewriting. It is declined on the continuation. Matthew's clause completes as 'do not your alms before men, to be seen of them'; Benjamin's completes as 'do not transgress, that the name be not blotted out of your hearts'. The one is a warning against performing righteousness publicly, the other a warning against breaking covenant, and nothing in Mosiah 5 is about display. This is the window closing one word early, in its purest form: the six shared words are an imperative frame the KJV happens to use once, and the seventh word is where the two verses part.

Jeremiah 31:33 is the obvious candidate for anything written in a heart, and its New Testament quotation at Hebrews 8:10 makes this look like a mediation question worth running. It was run and it decided nothing: the two forms differ at 'law in their inward parts' against 'laws into their mind', and Mosiah 5:12 reproduces neither. The reason is that Mosiah is not writing the law in the heart at all. What is written is a NAME — 'retain the name written always in your hearts' — and the KJV writes a name on a person in exactly one place, Revelation 14:1, where it is written in the forehead. The link is placed there, with 2 Corinthians 3:3 for the writing surface. Jeremiah 31 remains the passage a reader should have in mind and is registered so that they do.

A typological expectation pulling toward a link the wording will not bear. Benjamin's illustration is a legal casus about a stray animal, and the KJV has exactly one cluster of statutes on stray animals — Exodus 23:4-5 and Deuteronomy 22:1-4 — so a reader trained on the Covenant Code will reach for it, especially since Mosiah 4:28 has just borrowed Exodus 22:14 verbatim. It does not hold. The statutes require the finder to bring the animal back to its owner; Benjamin's man drives it away and casts it out, and approves of doing so. The shared vocabulary is one word, 'ass', which the KJV uses ninety times. The verse's expulsion language is Matthew 22:13's and the link is written there. Job 24:3's 'they drive away the ass of the fatherless' shares two more words and is likewise declined: in Job the driving away is the crime, and in Mosiah it is the right response of an honest man to an animal he does not know.

'In heaven and in earth' scored highest of the six candidates the machine returned for this verse, and four of them share the same run — Daniel 6:27, Philippians 2:10, Psalm 135:6, Matthew 28:18. That is the definition of a formula: a phrase distributed widely enough that its presence identifies nothing. The verse's borrowings are elsewhere in it, at 1 Corinthians 15:58, Revelation 19:6 and Ephesians 1:13/3:9, and the creation doxology is the Book of Mormon's own, used already at Mosiah 4:9.

'That which is to come' is connective English for the future and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly, including at 4:11 in the previous chapter. Revelation 1:4's 'him which is, and which was, and which is to come' is a divine title, not a temporal adverbial, and 1 Timothy 4:8's is the life to come as against the present one. Neither is in view in 'great views of that which is to come'.

The title is adjudicated at Mosiah 3:5, where it first enters the sermon in the angel's own words; 5:15 is the same speaker (Benjamin) using his own now-established title at the sermon's close, one of five recurrences (3:5, 3:17, 3:18, 3:21, 5:2) tracked there. Registered here, rather than left silent, because 5:15 happens to reproduce the exact three-word Revelation 19:6 sequence 'Lord God Omnipotent' most precisely of all six occurrences — a reader who notices that should be sent to 3:5, not shown nothing.
